data.title: Does the timing of mTOR inhibition have to match the body's own pulses — feeding, exercise, sleep?
data.gap: Intermittent dosing is currently justified as a way to lower exposure and dodge side effects. But if the pathway reads pattern rather than level, the interesting variable is not how often the drug is given but whether the drug's troughs line up with the body's own peaks — the post-meal window, the post-exercise anabolic window, the circadian trough. We found no lifespan study that varied the phase of dosing while holding the dose and the interval constant (PubMed search, October 2026: rapamycin or everolimus combined with time-of-day, circadian or chronotherapy). Dosing time has been varied for other endpoints in mice: everolimus given when tumour mTOR activity peaked improved survival of tumour-bearing mice (OKA2013), and everolimus toxicity to the immune system and testes depended on time of day (Ozturk, Chronobiol Int 2018, PMID 29400578; Eur J Pharm Sci 2021, PMID 34242751).
data.gap_beginner: Giving the drug once a week instead of daily is usually explained as a way to lower the dose and avoid side effects. But if the pathway cares about rhythm, the question is not how often you give it — it is whether the gaps in the drug line up with the moments the body actually needs the pathway on, like after a meal or after exercise. We found no study that tested this alignment for ageing or lifespan. In mice, the time of day the drug was given did change how well it worked against a tumour and how many side effects it caused.
data.changed_since_written: The one head-to-head schedule comparison in exercising mice found that weekly and thrice-weekly rapamycin both preserved hypertrophy and grip strength, and that the schedule mattered for glucose rather than for muscle (Elliehausen, Aging Cell 2025, PMID 40704394). That is evidence that schedule does something, and a hint that the usual reason given for choosing a schedule may not be the variable that decides muscle outcomes. Intermittent dosing has also now shown lifespan extension in its own right, in female C57BL/6J mice (Arriola Apelo, J Gerontol A 2016, PMID 27091134).
data.still_open: Phase, as distinct from frequency. Does the same weekly dose given before against after the feeding window, or before against after exercise, produce different lifespan, muscle and glucose outcomes? This is a cheap experiment by ageing-research standards and it has not been run.
data.why_it_matters: It is the practical form of F1 and it is testable now with existing drugs. If phase matters, current human trials have not controlled a variable that could change the answer.
data.how_to_test: A lifespan cohort at one dose and one interval, with dosing phase as the only variable — aligned with the light-phase trough, aligned with the feeding window, aligned post-exercise. Endpoints: lifespan, grip strength and contractile force, glucose tolerance, and mTORC1 and mTORC2 substrate phosphorylation sampled at several times of day rather than once.

gap_status.label: Probable gap
gap_status.basis: One logged PubMed search, October 2026 (rapamycin or everolimus combined with time-of-day, circadian or chronotherapy) found no lifespan study that varied the phase of dosing. PubMed only; preprints and trial registries were not searched.
